items.q: What's the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?

options.t: What the system does, versus how well it must do it
options.why: Right. 'Upload a photo' is functional. 'Feed loads in under 200ms for 100M daily users' is non-functional — and it's the non-functional list that actually shapes the architecture.

options.t: Functional covers backend behavior; non-functional covers the frontend
options.why: Nothing to do with frontend vs backend. Both lists describe the whole system — one says what it does, the other says how well it must do it.

options.t: Functional = required features; non-functional = optional nice-to-haves
options.why: Tempting, because 'non-functional' sounds like 'not needed.' It's the opposite — 'never lose a message' is non-functional and utterly mandatory.

options.t: They're two names for the same list
options.why: They're different lists with different jobs. Mixing them up means your design decisions have nothing to hang on — scale targets live in the non-functional list.

items.q: In the 45-minute skeleton, which phase most strongly decides whether you're graded senior?

options.t: The deep dives
options.why: Yes. Requirements through high-level design qualify you; the 15-20 minutes of deep dives — chosen by you, unprompted — decide the level. 'The deep dive is what separates L5 from L4.'

options.t: The requirements phase
options.why: Scoping well matters and sloppy scoping hurts, but everyone competent does requirements. It's table stakes, not the differentiator.

options.t: The API design
options.why: The API section should be quick and unremarkable. Gold-plating it actually costs you deep-dive time, which is where the level is decided.

options.t: The estimation math
options.why: Estimation is required at senior, but it's a supporting act — numbers exist to feed decisions. The judgment on display in deep dives is what gets graded.

items.q: What does this book call 'the crux' of a design problem?

options.t: The one genuinely hard part the question was invented to probe
options.why: Exactly. Most of any system is routine. The crux is the burning room — ID collisions in a URL shortener, celebrity fanout in a feed. Finding it fast and saying so is a top senior signal.

options.t: The component that will cost the most to run in production
options.why: Cost matters, but the crux is about difficulty, not price. The hard part is often cheap to run and hard to get correct.

options.t: The database schema, since data decisions are hardest to reverse
options.why: The schema is usually one of the routine parts. Occasionally the crux involves data modeling, but the crux is defined by difficulty, not by layer.

options.t: The part the interviewer refuses to discuss
options.why: Backwards — the crux is the part the interviewer is quietly hoping you'll find. They lit the fire; they're waiting for you to smell smoke.

items.q: According to interviewers, the most common way candidates fail system design rounds is:

options.t: Never finishing a complete working design
options.why: Correct — and it surprises people. The #1 documented failure isn't lack of depth; it's running out of time with no end-to-end system. A request must be traceable all the way in and back out.

options.t: Not knowing enough technologies to name the right tool
options.why: Rarely the killer. Interviewers forgive gaps in tool trivia; they don't forgive an incomplete machine or absent judgment.

options.t: Making the design too simple
options.why: Justified simplicity reads senior. Over-engineering is the failure mode on this axis, not simplicity.

options.t: Spending too long on requirements
options.why: Pacing errors happen, but they're a symptom. The fatal outcome they cause is the real #1: an unfinished design.

items.q: What makes a back-of-envelope estimate 'good' in an interview?

options.t: It changes a design decision
options.why: Yes. '20:1 read-to-write ratio, so I design the read path first and lean on caching' — the number produced a conclusion. Math that changes nothing is filler, and seniors skip it.

options.t: It's accurate to two decimal places
options.why: Nobody cares about precision. Orders of magnitude and round numbers are expected; the grading is on whether the number connects to the design.

options.t: It uses impressive-sounding units
options.why: Petabytes-dropping without consequences reads as theater. A humble 'about 6K QPS, so one beefy database can't take this alone' beats it every time.

options.t: It's done silently to save time
options.why: Silent math earns zero credit — the reasoning out loud IS the deliverable. The interviewer grades the connection between number and decision.

items.q: 'Design a system you'd want to be on call for' is shorthand for:

options.t: Including monitoring, rollout, rollback, and failure handling
options.why: Right. Operational maturity — what you watch, how you ship changes safely, what happens at 3am — is now explicitly graded at senior, not a staff-level bonus.

options.t: Designing systems that never fail
options.why: Impossible, and claiming it is a red flag. The graded skill is designing for failure: detect it, contain it, recover from it.

options.t: Choosing boring, well-understood technologies over new ones
options.why: Boring tech is often wise, but that's a different principle. On-call readiness is about observability and failure plans, whatever the stack.

options.t: Adding redundancy at every layer so nothing is a single point of failure
options.why: Redundancy without measurement is just expensive hope. You can't be paged for — or debug — what you can't see; monitoring comes first.

items.q: Which behavior most clearly reads as mid-level rather than senior, even when the answers are technically correct?

options.t: Waiting for the interviewer to choose the deep dives
options.why: Yes — passivity is the tell. 'If you're looking to your interviewer for guidance about how to proceed, you're losing points.' Seniors propose their own deep-dive agenda.

options.t: Asking clarifying questions about scope
options.why: That's expected at every level — scoping questions early are a strength, not passivity.

options.t: Admitting you don't know something
options.why: Honest gaps, flagged and routed around, read as maturity. Bluffing is what kills.

options.t: Using simple, unfashionable technology choices
options.why: Simple, justified choices read senior. 'Postgres, because it won't be the bottleneck and I get transactions' is a strong answer.

items.q: Why should you state your scope out loud ('feed and upload; DMs out of scope — fair?') instead of just starting?

options.t: It turns a vague prompt into an agreed contract
options.why: Right. The vagueness is the test. Negotiating scope out loud is the graded skill — and it protects you from spending 45 minutes on the part they didn't care about.

options.t: It fills time while you think
options.why: It does buy thinking time, but that's a side effect. Treating it as filler misses that scoping is itself being graded.

options.t: It's a politeness ritual interviewers expect
options.why: Not politeness — engineering. Real projects die from unscoped ambiguity, and the interview is a compressed simulation of exactly that.

options.t: It stops the interviewer from moving the goalposts later
options.why: They can and will move the goalposts anyway ('now 100x the users') — that's deliberate. Scope agreement starts the game; it doesn't freeze it.

items.q: Interviewer: 'SQL or NoSQL for the user profiles?' Which reply reads most senior?

options.t: "Postgres — profiles are small, relational, and read-mostly. If reads dominate later, I'd add a cache before switching databases."
options.why: Commitment, a reason tied to the workload, a growth path, and a named alternative you consciously deferred. That's the full senior package in three sentences.

options.t: "Both are viable. SQL gives ACID and joins; NoSQL gives horizontal scale and flexible schemas. It depends on the requirements."
options.why: Everything here is true, and it commits to nothing. This is the option-listing pattern that explicitly reads as lacking judgment — 'it depends' with no decision is a non-answer.

options.t: "NoSQL. It scales horizontally, and at this company's size everything eventually needs to scale, so I'd start there."
options.why: A commitment, but justified by vibes. Profile data at this size doesn't need horizontal scale on day one, and 'everything must scale' is the buzzword-architecture tell.

options.t: "Whichever the team already runs — operational familiarity beats theoretical fit."
options.why: There's real wisdom in this line for actual jobs, but in the interview it dodges the design question being asked. Use the reasoning — then still make the call on the merits.

items.q: Twenty minutes in, you're still perfecting the API section of your Instagram design. What's the senior move?

options.t: Sketch the rest end-to-end fast, then deep-dive the feed path
options.why: Yes. Complete-then-deep is the winning shape. The API section can't earn you the level, but a missing end-to-end design can absolutely lose it.

options.t: Finish the API properly — a half-specified contract is worse than none
options.why: This is how strong engineers fail: polishing a low-signal section while the clock eats the deep dives. 'Never finished' is the #1 documented failure.

options.t: Ask the interviewer whether they'd like more API detail
options.why: Occasionally checking in is fine, but outsourcing your pacing decision is the waiting-to-be-led pattern. Own the clock.

options.t: Skip the high-level diagram and jump straight to a deep dive to save time
options.why: Deep-diving a component of a system that doesn't exist yet on the board leaves the interviewer with no complete machine to grade. Finish the loop first, however roughly.

items.q: You estimate a service at 300 requests/sec average. The senior follow-through is:

options.t: "Peak maybe 1K/sec — two app servers and one Postgres. Scale isn't the problem here; correctness is."
options.why: The number produced a conclusion — this system is small, so stop designing for imaginary scale and find the real crux. Estimation that redirects your attention is estimation doing its job.

options.t: "So we'll need Kafka for ingestion and a sharded database up front, so we never have to migrate later."
options.why: 300/sec needs none of that. Deploying big-scale machinery against small numbers is over-engineering — and it signals your estimates don't connect to your decisions.

options.t: "Round up to 1M/sec and design for that — better to over-provision than to redesign under pressure."
options.why: A 1000x 'safety margin' isn't conservative, it's abandoning the estimate. Design for realistic peak with headroom, and say what you'd change if you were wrong by 10x.

options.t: "Note the number, then move on to the architecture and revisit capacity at the end if time allows."
options.why: An estimate that changes nothing was filler. The whole point of the number is the sentence after it — what it means for the design.

items.q: You're asked to design a ticket-booking system. Which observation shows you've found the crux?

options.t: "The hard part is thousands of people grabbing the same seat at once — never selling one seat twice."
options.why: That's the fire. Concurrency on identical hot rows — not raw traffic — is what ticket-booking questions exist to probe. Announcing it and steering there is the senior pattern.

options.t: "The hard part is serving event pages and seat maps fast, so I'd put a CDN in front of everything."
options.why: True and trivial — static content is a solved, routine problem. Touring the room with curtains while the seat-selling room burns.

options.t: "The hard part is supporting many payment providers and currencies without coupling them to checkout."
options.why: A product feature, not a design challenge. Integration breadth isn't what the question is probing.

options.t: "The hard part is query speed — the seats table needs the right indexes or lookups crawl under load."
options.why: Correct and routine. Indexes are assumed competence — the interviewer's fire is the concurrent purchase of the same seat.

items.q: Mid-design, the interviewer says: 'Interesting — but what about when the message queue itself falls over?' What are they most likely doing?

options.t: Steering you toward a failure mode they want covered
options.why: Interviewer redirects are load-bearing. They're either rescuing you from a dead end or pointing at the signal they still need. Engaging genuinely earns collaboration points; brushing it off loses them.

options.t: Testing whether you will defend your design when challenged
options.why: Occasionally they probe conviction, but the default read of a redirect is 'please go here.' Fighting hints is a documented failure pattern — pushing back against a hint costs real points.

options.t: Signaling the interview is going badly
options.why: Usually the opposite — probing questions mean they're engaged and collecting signal. Silence is the scary sound.

options.t: Filling time because you finished early
options.why: Failure-mode questions ARE the senior evaluation, not padding. This moment is the exam, arriving on schedule.

items.q: You have 3 minutes left and a complete design on the board. The strongest way to spend them:

options.t: "Ops pass: watch p99, error rate, queue depth; ship behind a flag by region; rollback is flipping it off."
options.why: The thirty-second habit that closes the biggest senior gap. Monitoring + rollout + rollback, concretely named, converts 'good design' into 'design I'd be on call for.'

options.t: Add caching layers at the edge and in front of the database, and show where they'd cut read load
options.why: Unrequested complexity in the final minutes reads as decoration. The unclaimed points are in operations, not more boxes.

options.t: Recap the whole design end to end so the interviewer leaves with a clear picture of the system
options.why: A pure recap adds zero new signal. A ten-second summary is fine — but spend the minutes on something not yet graded.

options.t: Ask how the design compares to what they run in production, to show curiosity about their stack
options.why: Puts them in an awkward spot and burns your closing window. Spend it demonstrating on-call thinking instead.

items.q: Which non-functional requirement, stated early, does the most work in a chat-app design?

options.t: "Once the server acknowledges a message, it is never lost"
options.why: This one sentence forces durable storage before acknowledgment, retries, and delivery guarantees — it generates half the architecture. That's what a load-bearing requirement looks like.

options.t: "The UI should feel modern and clean"
options.why: Real product concern, zero architectural consequence in this round. It shapes no backend decision.

options.t: "The system should use microservices, not a monolith"
options.why: An architecture choice cosplaying as a requirement. Requirements say what must be true; the design decides how. Starting from 'must use microservices' is backwards.

options.t: "Code should be well-documented"
options.why: Engineering hygiene, not a system property. It won't change a single box on the whiteboard.

items.q: The interviewer asks 'why Redis over Memcached here?' The senior-reading answer is:

options.t: "Redis — I need sorted sets for this leaderboard and persistence across restarts. Memcached would do for flat caching."
options.why: Specific features tied to this design's needs, plus an honest statement of when the alternative wins. Opinion backed by mechanism is exactly what 'experience-based specificity' means.

options.t: "Redis is more popular, better maintained, and has a much larger community writing about it."
options.why: Popularity is not a mechanism. This is name-dropping without familiarity — the pattern interviewers explicitly flag.

options.t: "Either works — they're both in-memory key-value caches, so I'd pick whichever ops already knows."
options.why: Shrugging at a direct trade-off question is option-listing at its worst — the question was an invitation to show depth, declined.

options.t: "Memcached is legacy at this point; nobody picks it for new systems, so Redis by default."
options.why: False (it still backs enormous fleets at Meta, among others) and dismissive — a confident wrong claim is worse than an honest gap.

items.q: Two candidates answer the same feed-design question. A: flawless textbook coverage of push vs pull fanout, ending 'both approaches have merit.' B: rougher delivery, but commits — 'push by default, pull above a million followers, because the read/write ratio is 20:1' — and volunteers 'my weak point is thundering herds when a celebrity posts; here's how I'd contain it.' Who gets the senior grade, and why?

options.t: B — commitment with reasons, plus self-identified weaknesses
options.why: B displays ownership: decides, ties the decision to a measured ratio, and critiques their own design unprompted — 'proactively recognize limitations' is verbatim senior rubric. A knows things; B decides things.

options.t: A — completeness and technical accuracy are the foundation of the grade
options.why: A's knowledge is real but ends in 'both have merit' — the exact hedge that caps candidates at mid-level. Knowledge without commitment grades as a book report.

options.t: Both equally — they covered the same material
options.why: The rubric doesn't grade material covered; it grades judgment displayed. Same facts, different behaviors, different levels.

options.t: B, but only because admitting weakness earns honesty points
options.why: Partial credit: the self-critique matters, but as evidence of an owner's mindset — someone thinking about how their system fails — not as a virtue bonus. The commitment plus the reason does the heavy lifting.

items.q: Designing an internal tool for 10,000 records updated a few times a day, a candidate proposes Elasticsearch, Kafka, and three service tiers 'for future scale.' The senior-calibrated alternative is:

options.t: "Keep all 10K records in memory, refresh periodically, scan linearly — and name the signal that would change that."
options.why: Ruthlessly cutting complexity, with a named escalation trigger, is a top-of-rubric senior behavior. 10K records is nothing; a linear scan wins. Simplicity chosen consciously and monitored reads as maturity.

options.t: The proposal is right — over-provisioning now beats a painful migration once the data grows
options.why: Complexity without justification reads as immaturity at the senior-plus bar. Every component is an on-call burden; buying three of them against imaginary load is a cost with no benefit.

options.t: Keep Elasticsearch for search but drop Kafka, since there's no real streaming requirement yet
options.why: Half the over-engineering is still over-engineering. The workload fits in memory on one machine — the honest design acknowledges that.

options.t: Ask the interviewer whether future scale is in scope before committing to a simpler design
options.why: Reasonable question, wrong crutch — the numbers already answered it. When the data speaks, deferring to the interviewer is the waiting-to-be-led pattern.

items.q: Interviewer: 'Your design works. Now 100x the users.' Your database shards are suddenly hot. The strongest response pattern is:

options.t: "Good — hot user-shard keys melt first. Cache in front now; reshard on a compound key later, at the cost of scatter-gather reads."
options.why: Naming the failure order, a containment move, a structural fix, and its cost — calmly, as if you expected the question — is precisely what the 100x push exists to elicit. Your design breaking IS the interview working.

options.t: "The design already handles it — every tier is horizontally scalable, so we add machines and move on."
options.why: Deflecting the stress test defends the design instead of exploring it. 'Horizontally scalable' as an incantation, without naming what actually breaks, is a buzzword shield — and interviewers push through it.

options.t: "I'd move to a managed cloud database that handles resharding and hot keys for us automatically."
options.why: Outsourcing the question isn't answering it. Managed services move the problem; the interviewer wants to see you reason about the hot-key mechanics wherever they live.

options.t: "I'd start the design over with a bigger architecture built for this scale from the beginning."
options.why: Throwing away a working design under pressure reads as panic. Evolve it: contain, then restructure, naming costs. Iteration under fire is the graded skill.

items.q: Which closing statement converts a good performance into a senior one?

options.t: "Before we wrap: I'd watch feed p99, fanout queue depth, and cache hit rate; ship behind a flag to 1%; the notification path is what I'd redesign first."
options.why: Ops instrumentation for THIS design, a safe rollout plan, and a self-identified weak point — three senior signals in twenty seconds, all unprompted. This closing alone can move a grade.

options.t: "So that's my design — happy to go deeper on any part of it that you'd like to explore further."
options.why: Polite, passive, and empty-handed. It hands your remaining signal-generation time back to the interviewer — the waiting-to-be-led pattern in miniature.

options.t: "This is close to how Instagram actually does it, so the approach is already battle-tested at scale."
options.why: Borrowed authority isn't judgment. The interviewer graded your reasoning, not Instagram's — and claiming their architecture invites probes you may not survive.

options.t: "With more time I'd add multi-region failover, a GraphQL layer, and a service mesh for the internals."
options.why: A wishlist of unjustified complexity as a closing note reads as decoration, not judgment. One weak point named honestly beats three technologies named ambitiously.

items.q: A candidate opens the deep-dive phase with: 'The interesting problem here is the write path under contention — I want to spend our remaining time there. The read path is standard caching, which I'm happy to sketch but not dwell on.' What did they just do?

options.t: Claimed the driver's seat and triaged by difficulty
options.why: They proposed the agenda (driving), identified the crux (triage), and consciously deprioritized the routine part while showing they know it's there. This single sentence pattern is trainable and worth practicing verbatim.

options.t: Took a gamble — the interviewer may have wanted the read path instead
options.why: It's a soft claim, not a decree — any interviewer who wants the read path will simply say so, and following that steer costs nothing. The expected value of proposing an agenda is strongly positive; passivity has no upside.

options.t: Showed off — announcing what's 'standard' sounds arrogant
options.why: Tone matters, but classifying problems by difficulty is the job. 'This part is routine, that part is hard' is engineering triage, and stated matter-of-factly it reads as calibration, not arrogance.

options.t: Wasted time on meta-commentary instead of designing
options.why: Ten seconds of agenda-setting multiplies the value of the next fifteen minutes and is itself graded behavior — the interviewer literally scores who drives.

items.q: Honest self-assessment: you realize mid-interview that the component you're deep-diving is one you've never actually operated. The senior move is:

options.t: "I haven't run Cassandra in production — reasoning from its design: writes are cheap, reads need tuning, so I'd validate the read path first."
options.why: Playing to strengths while flagging what you don't know is explicit rubric language. First-principles reasoning from an honest base earns more than fluent recitation — and infinitely more than a bluff that collapses under one probe.

options.t: Bluff through it — admitting you've never run it at a senior interview undercuts everything else
options.why: Backwards. One probing follow-up exposes the bluff and poisons trust in everything else you've said. Interviewers report honest gaps as neutral-to-positive; discovered bluffs as terminal.

options.t: Pivot the deep dive to a component you know better, and steer discussion back to your strengths
options.why: A visible flinch — and it wastes the setup you've built. Often the honest first-principles path through the current component is stronger than a jarring pivot. (Choosing familiar ground BEFORE diving is smart; fleeing mid-dive is not.)

options.t: Ask the interviewer to pick a different area, since they know which parts they want to hear about
options.why: Hands them the wheel at the worst moment. You can redirect yourself if needed — outsourcing the rescue is the passivity pattern again.
